title: Illusions of Knowledge
coreMove: Catch the moment a coherent explanation stops feeling like a hypothesis and starts feeling like settled fact — before the evidence has earned that certainty.
sourcePressure: Archie Cochrane pushed medicine toward randomized testing because professional confidence was treated as sufficient evidence. He was then harmed by the same error when a specialist delivered certainty before pathology results arrived. The chapter's core threat is not ignorance but the premature closure that fluency produces.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The wrong version is a catalog of cognitive biases (confirmation bias, availability heuristic, etc.). The chapter's precise target is explanatory overreach: the moment you stop treating your explanation as a candidate and start treating it as a verdict — and how that internal shift happens without feeling like an error.

sourceAnchors.name: Archie Cochrane
sourceAnchors.detail: Scottish physician and epidemiologist who spent his career arguing that medicine relied too heavily on expert opinion and clinical intuition, pushing for randomized controlled trials as the standard — later became a patient himself when a specialist diagnosed him with a terminal cancer before pathology results were in; the diagnosis turned out to be wrong
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Cochrane had spent forty years demanding that medicine test its confident claims — then a specialist gave him a cancer verdict before the biopsy came back, and the verdict was wrong.

hook: opening with a list of cognitive biases — wrong chapter identity
opening with 'Do you ever feel overconfident?' — coaching register, too vague
counterintuition: 'The smarter you are, the more confident you are — and that's the problem' — misses the book's narrower point about evidence not keeping pace with confidence
tryThisNow: 'Write down three things you believe but can't prove' — generic epistemology prompt, not chapter-specific
any prompt about 'being more humble' without a specific mechanism for checking evidence
examples: any example where someone is simply overconfident without the specific beat of an explanation feeling complete before evidence arrives
medical malpractice framing — the chapter is not about negligence but about a cognitive transition that happens to thoughtful people

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: The chapter is about premature closure — the examples should demonstrate variety in how closure happens, which requires variety in how each scene enters

exampleSpecs.domain: structural engineering firm diagnosing a crack in a parking garage before materials lab results return
exampleSpecs.audience: a senior structural engineer whose confident explanation has already been shared with building management
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the building is evacuated immediately or allowed to remain open while the lab report comes back
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the engineer has written a confident internal memo explaining the crack as a routine shrinkage fracture — and realizes she wrote it on the basis of what the crack looks like, not what the lab will find; she has to decide whether to mark it provisional before it circulates further
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a thin diagonal fracture running through a concrete pillar, photographed under fluorescent light
mustInclude: the internal memo already written and sent
the specific moment she notices her explanation feels settled
the lab results still 48 hours away
mustAvoid: framing it as negligence — the engineer is competent, just premature

exampleSpecs.domain: elementary school vice principal explaining a student's reading difficulty before the psychoeducational assessment is complete
exampleSpecs.audience: a vice principal who has spoken to parents and shaped their expectations around an explanation that felt obvious
exampleSpecs.stakes: the parents' willingness to pursue a full assessment vs. accepting the simple narrative
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the vice principal gave the parents a crisp explanation — 'he's likely just a late bloomer, we see this often' — before the psychoeducational assessment came back showing a significant processing disorder; the explanation had colonized the room before it had any right to
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a parent meeting where the vice principal's confident, reassuring manner has closed down the parents' questions
mustInclude: the VP's explanation given before any formal assessment
the assessment revealing something the explanation missed
mustAvoid: making the VP incompetent — she was being kind and plausible, not reckless

exampleSpecs.domain: auto mechanic diagnosing an intermittent electrical fault without running the full diagnostic scan
exampleSpecs.audience: a mechanic who is expert enough to have a confident story ready before the scan runs
exampleSpecs.stakes: the customer's repair cost and whether the real fault is found on the first visit
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the mechanic has already told the service advisor 'almost certainly the alternator' based on the symptom pattern — the diagnostic scan returns fifteen minutes later showing a corroded grounding strap, which is cheaper and simpler; the confident early explanation had primed everyone including himself
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a service bay with the hood up and a mechanic with an explanation already forming before the scan finishes
mustInclude: the early verbal explanation already given
the diagnostic scan result contradicting it
the subtle cost of the premature explanation (parts already ordered)
mustAvoid: making this an incompetence story — pattern recognition is legitimate, premature closure is the error

exampleSpecs.domain: a market analyst explaining a stock decline with a narrative that feels complete before earnings data is released
exampleSpecs.audience: a buy-side analyst who has circulated an explanation to portfolio managers before the full earnings release
exampleSpecs.stakes: the investment team's positioning based on an explanation that turned out to be directionally wrong
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the analyst sent a confident note explaining the 8% decline as supply-chain pressure — the earnings call the next day revealed the decline was entirely a one-time tax charge with no structural implication; the explanation had been plausible enough to feel true before the evidence arrived
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a morning report email sent at 7:42 a.m. with the subject line 'What's happening with [ticker]'
mustInclude: the circulated explanation before the earnings call
the specific mismatch on the actual cause
the downstream positioning decision made on the explanation
mustAvoid: any implication the analyst should have known — the point is the inner posture of settled certainty

exampleSpecs.domain: a forensic investigator explaining a warehouse fire's cause before the accelerant lab results return
exampleSpecs.audience: an investigator whose verbal explanation to the insurance adjuster felt so complete that written follow-up seemed redundant
exampleSpecs.stakes: a $2 million insurance claim and a potential arson referral to prosecutors
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the investigator's confident oral explanation (faulty wiring) was accepted and the claim was moving toward settlement — the accelerant test returned three days later positive for ignition fuel; the explanation had been offered as if certainty were already established
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a charred beam photographed as evidence, with the investigator's handwriting in the margin of the site notes: 'wiring failure — consistent with pattern'
mustInclude: the oral explanation given as near-certain
the insurance adjuster's acceptance of it
mustAvoid: framing this as fraud or misconduct — the investigator was competent but premature

exampleSpecs.domain: a family physician explaining a patient's fatigue before bloodwork results are in
exampleSpecs.audience: a physician who has already reassured the patient and documented a preliminary diagnosis
exampleSpecs.stakes: a patient who will or will not pursue further testing based on how settled the doctor's explanation sounded
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the physician's charted note reads 'probable overwork syndrome, recommend rest' — the bloodwork returns showing a thyroid deficiency that explains everything; the note had settled the case before the evidence arrived, and the patient had started 'resting' instead of treating
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a patient chart with the physician's neat handwriting recording a confident but provisional diagnosis as if it were final
mustInclude: the patient already acting on it before bloodwork
the bloodwork result that reopens what felt closed
mustAvoid: making it a misdiagnosis liability scene — the point is about inner epistemic state, not error rate

skillTargets: identify the specific moment explanatory overreach occurs in a scenario
apply the proportionality rule (confidence should match evidence) to a new domain
distinguish illusion of knowledge from simple error or ignorance
analyze what signals indicate an explanation has prematurely closed
evaluate whether a confident claim has passed the randomized-evidence standard or just passed the plausibility test

tryThisNowSpec: Take the next explanation you're about to give — to a colleague, client, or family member — and ask yourself one question before you say it: what piece of evidence, if it came back differently than expected, would change this explanation? If you cannot name that piece of evidence, your explanation has already closed before it should have. State it as provisional.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one passage that asks the reader directly whether they have ever given an explanation that felt finished — not as a reflection prompt but as a sharp diagnostic question that the Cochrane example then answers
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
